UK investors are watching the AI boom run into funding roadblocks, as seen with Microsoft walking away from a major British data centre deal. Big projects can stall when debt markets get tougher. Yet smaller listed businesses with cleaner balance sheets still have room to move. This article picks out three financially solid low priced UK stocks that aim to give you exposure without relying on heavy borrowing.

The three stocks highlighted here offer a compelling starting point if you want exposure to lower risk early-stage businesses backed by sturdier finances. However, if you want the strongest names, these 16 elite penny stocks are at the top of the list.

Baltic Classifieds Group (LSE:BCG)

Baltic Classifieds Group runs leading online portals for car, property, job, services and general classifieds across the Baltics, with auto listings generating about €31 million, real estate €26 million, jobs and services €17 million and generalist sites €14 million, and the group valued at roughly €995 million.

For a screener focused on financially fit penny stocks, Baltic Classifieds Group offers something more tangible than a story stock. Core revenue is anchored in everyday car and property listings that users keep returning to when they need to transact.

Rapid rollout of AI and data driven tools, such as smart pricing, salary estimators, fraud screening and lead management, is enhancing platform utility for buyers and sellers, which can help justify ongoing price increases and support EBIT and EBITDA.

What happens to this earnings profile if one quiet change in how those listings are priced and packaged shifts the margin picture again?

That pricing shift is the crux of the story, and the full narrative for Baltic Classifieds Group shows how Baltic Classifieds Group could see margins decoupling from simple listing volume.

LSE:BCG Revenue & Expenses Breakdown as at Oct 2026
Ashmore Group (LSE:ASHM)

Ashmore Group runs emerging markets equity and bond funds that give you indirect exposure to smaller or lower priced issuers, and earns £139.3 million from investment management fees within a business valued at about £1.47b.

Ashmore Group offers a different route into the Financially Fit Penny Stocks theme, since you are effectively backing a specialist manager that picks through smaller or lower priced emerging markets issuers on your behalf rather than owning each security directly.

Ashmore Group has a long record of seed capital gains, including a large £82.5m contribution in FY26. A moderation in realized gains from this portfolio could remove an important support for profit before tax and leave reported earnings more dependent on subdued core fee income.

When investing in tech exchange-traded funds (ETFs), sometimes it's a good idea to peek under the hood and see what you're really buying within each fund's portfolio. Sometimes there is a lot of overlap from one tech ETF to another. This can make it easier to choose the best tech ETF for your goals, based on which fund holds which mix of stocks and sectors.

The Vanguard Information Technology ETF (NYSEMKT: VGT) is a popular tech fund that holds 318 stocks. It represents a wide range of companies in the electronics and computer industries, including semiconductors, software, hardware, and tech-related services and components. And VGT is a passive index fund, so it doesn't pick stocks -- it just tracks the performance of its tech sector benchmark.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

When you buy VGT, you're going to get a strong concentration of major tech names that are also top holdings in the S&P 500 index (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) and Nasdaq-100 index. But how much of VGT is just a few major tech stocks that you can buy in other ETFs?

A large percentage of assets of the Vanguard Information Technology ETF is made up of only four big-name tech tickers: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), and Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO). As of Sept. 30, those four stocks represented about 49% of the VGT fund's assets.

If you feel like VGT is getting too top-heavy with just these four tech names, or you want to own a different mix of stocks, this could affect your investment choices. Let's take a closer look at VGT and its concentration of tech majors NVDA, AAPL, MSFT, and AVGO.

Image source: Getty Images.
Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT): 22 years of 15% annualized returns

The Vanguard Information Technology ETF has delivered strong returns for investors, with average annual returns of 15.03% since the fund's inception in January 2004. It's done even better in the past few years, with about 24.7% annualized returns in the past 10 years, 20.9% in the past five years, 35% in the past three years, and about 35.2% in the past year.

Unlike many popular tech ETFs, VGT is somewhat unique for some of the well-known "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks that it does not own. For example, the VGT fund does not hold Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, or Tesla. That's because although these companies are frequently described as "tech stocks," they are not technically part of the information technology sector as defined by the MSCI US IMI Information Technology 25/50 Index, which is the benchmark that VGT follows.

title: Where Will Microsoft Stock Be in 2030?
detail:
Where Will Microsoft Stock Be in 2030?
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 18, 2026 at 1:43 AM MST 5 min read
MSFT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Shares of Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) closed at a record $543.45 on Oct. 13 and slipped about 2% a day later, finishing Oct. 14 at $533.69. The software giant's next earnings report, for its fiscal 2027 first quarter, is due Oct. 28.

My prediction is that Microsoft stock will trade near $730 by the middle of 2030. Specifically, it's my estimate of the price on June 30, 2030, when Microsoft's fiscal 2030 ends. It assumes non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share rise about 13% a year from here, and that investors pay about 26 times those earnings then.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

That price would be around 37% over the stock's Oct. 14 close, or about 9% a year before dividends. And it needs Microsoft's earnings to rise at just a bit over half the rate they managed last fiscal year.

Image source: Getty Images.

A solid starting point

For the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2026, Microsoft boosted adjusted earnings per share 22% to $17.28. The adjusted number strips out gains and losses on the company's investment in OpenAI.

Notably, growth didn't slow as the year went on. Against the year-ago periods, adjusted earnings per share rose 24% in the fiscal second quarter of 2026 (the period ended Dec. 31, 2025), then 21% in fiscal Q3 and 23% in fiscal Q4. Full-year revenue was $331.8 billion, up 18%, and operating income climbed 21%.

The full-year number also includes a $3.2 billion gain on Microsoft's investment in Anthropic, booked in fiscal Q4. If anything, then, the $17.28 starting point might be a bit generous.

Spending may slow earnings growth

But I don't expect 22% growth to hold. The biggest reason is the cost of building data centers for artificial intelligence.

Microsoft's spending on property and equipment totaled around $116 billion in fiscal 2026, up about 80% from about $65 billion the year before. That spending hits the income statement over time as depreciation, and the charge is already climbing faster than sales. The line on Microsoft's cash flow statement for depreciation, amortization, and other items rose 31% to $38.5 billion last fiscal year, well above 18% revenue growth. And the spending keeps rising. Fiscal Q4's additions to property and equipment were $35.8 billion, over double the year-ago quarter's $17.1 billion.

True, Microsoft is extending the estimated useful lives of its data centers and office buildings from 15 years to 25 years, which spreads out some of that cost. But management said the change should have just a minimal benefit to fiscal 2027 operating income.

title: UBS resets Microsoft stock price target for investors
detail:
UBS resets Microsoft stock price target for investors
Hillary Remy, Celine Provini
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 7:37 AM MST 5 min read
MSFT
UBS
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Not long ago, Microsoft looked like one of Big Tech's laggards. Its shares were down more than 20% for the year heading into its late July earnings report.

Then Azure grew 43%, and the stock surged 9% the next day.

Analysts are now scrambling to catch up. Ahead of the company's next report, a string of Wall Street firms, including TD Cowen, Mizuho and Citi, raised their price targets, and UBS made the biggest jump of the group.

Also read: Morgan Stanley finds a new twist in Microsoft's AI story

UBS raises Microsoft stock target from $525 to $675

UBS raised its Microsoft price target to $675 from $525 and kept a Buy rating. Analyst Karl Kierstead noted that the shares have rallied 39% since the June quarter report and returned 30% over the past six months, leaving the stock near its 52-week high.

UBS made the call ahead of the company's fiscal first-quarter report, due Oct. 28, according to Investing.com.

UBS admits the trade is getting crowded. It called Microsoft a "consensus long position," with investors now expecting more from Azure and Microsoft 365. Still, the firm said "the fundamentals support those higher expectations" and argued the stock's valuation at 23 times calendar 2027 earnings "is not stretched."

Azure is doing the heavy lifting. The cloud business grew 43% in the June quarter and crossed $100 billion in annualized revenue, and management guided for about 45% growth in the September quarter. Revenue in the broader Intelligent Cloud segment rose 32% to $39.3 billion, as reported by TheStreet.

Demand is still running ahead of supply. Microsoft said "customer demand for Azure remained higher than available capacity," while its commercial backlog jumped 84% to $678 billion.

Excluding OpenAI, that backlog still grew 25%, and Microsoft 365 Copilot now has well over 30 million paid seats.

UBS raised its Microsoft price target to $675 from $525 and kept a Buy rating.Bloomberg / Getty Images
UBS is not alone in bullish Microsoft view

Other firms are lining up behind the same story.

TD Cowen raised its target to $625 from $540 and sees the potential for a "higher than normal" Azure beat, pointing to third-party data that screened as the strongest in history, a full quarter of its Fairwater data center, and a bullish read on OpenAI's growth.

The upgrades kept coming from there. Mizuho lifted its target to $600 from $510 after channel checks it called "very healthy overall," while Citi raised its target to $636 from $600, citing survey and reseller checks that point to faster growth in productivity software and public cloud. Citi also ranks Microsoft among the best-positioned AI vendors.

Here's How Microsoft's $175 Billion in Capital Expenditures Is Hurting Its Business
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

NVDA
OPAI.PVT

Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) is among the big three cloud computing infrastructure providers and is always included in any list of AI hyperscalers. It's heavily pursuing a massive amount of AI computing power for its internal service, Copilot, while also powering other products like OpenAI's ChatGPT through its cloud computing platform, Azure.

To support this growth, Microsoft is investing heavily in data centers. This year alone, it expects its capital expenditures to hit $175 billion, with most of that going toward constructing and equipping data centers. That is leading to strong growth, but what if this growth is actually hurting its business?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

While it may sound odd, Microsoft's business is actually being harmed by the heavy pursuit of its cloud computing empire. Here's why.

Image source: Getty Images.
Microsoft is spending big

At first, you may imagine that the reason that these capital expenditures are hurting Microsoft is that it could be spending that $175 billion in ways that generate a more direct return for shareholders, such as on share buybacks or dividends. But that's not what I'm talking about. In fact, I'm OK with Microsoft spending big on AI because it needs to evolve its business to adapt to the AI age or risk being left behind.

Moreover, Microsoft's spending is resulting in strong growth. Azure saw its revenue rise 43% during its latest quarter, passing a $100 billion annual run rate. Additionally, Copilot reached 30 million paid seats, indicating strong adoption of the proprietary AI platform. Overall, Microsoft's revenue rose 18% last quarter.

While that's impressive for a company that's as large as Microsoft, there's a major caveat.

Azure's operating margin likely isn't as good as the rest of Microsoft's business

Unfortunately for investors, Microsoft doesn't publicly break out detailed statistics for its individual segments, such as Azure's operating margins. However, Azure's chief competitors, Amazon Web Services (AWS) (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Google Cloud from Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), freely share that information. It's unlikely that Microsoft Azure's margins are much different from theirs, since they operate using essentially the same business model. During the most recent quarter, Google Cloud's operating margin was 36% while AWS' was 39%. So, I think it's highly likely that Azure's operating margins are in the high-30% range.
